wrong: a woman walking in a city
right: a 30-year-old woman, shoulder-length red curly hair, tan trench coat, walking steadily forward down a rain-slicked street at dusk — same face and outfit held for the full clip
never: Never leave a recurring character’s appearance undescribed after the first shot. Undescribed features are the #1 cause of face and identity drift between frames.

right: locked-off static tripod shot, no camera movement, subject enters frame left and exits frame right
never: Never stack more than one camera movement — pan, zoom, dolly — in a single generation. Stacked motions are what cause warping and geometry smearing.

wrong: she spins around quickly in a floral dress, hair flying
right: she turns her head slowly, 90 degrees over 2 seconds, plain solid-colored top, minimal hair movement, no spinning or rapid motion
never: Never pair fast or rotational motion with high-detail textures, patterns, or loose hair/fabric in the same shot. That combination is the single biggest cause of warping — the model can’t track fine detail fast enough and the geometry smears and melts.

right: dense pine forest, tall trees with visible bark texture, soft overcast light, camera fixed so the treeline stays constant through the whole shot
never: Never describe a background in one vague word for any shot over 3 seconds. Vague backgrounds get redrawn from scratch every few frames — that’s morphing scenery.

right: single warm key light, camera left, 45° angle, fixed 3200K color temperature, no lighting change for the duration of the clip
never: Never omit a light source and color temperature from the prompt. A missing lighting direction is the leading cause of flicker between frames.

right: she reaches with her right hand, wraps four fingers around the handle, lifts it 6 inches straight up at a slow even pace, wrist steady
never: Never describe a hand-object interaction in fewer than one full clause. Under-specified hand actions are the top cause of melting fingers and object clipping.

wrong: make it look cinematic and artistic
right: 35mm film grain, muted teal-and-orange grade, shallow depth of field at f/2.8, held constant across every frame
never: Never let “cinematic” stand alone as a style instruction. The model has no fixed definition of it and will reinterpret it shot to shot — that’s style drift.

wrong: a person walks across a room
right: a person walks across a room — no text overlays, no extra limbs, no camera cuts, no background characters, no motion blur on the face
never: Never submit a generation with zero exclusion terms. An empty negative prompt leaves every known failure mode on the table.

right: one continuous action at a natural, even pace across the full clip — a single action per generation, nothing more
never: Never request more than one major action inside a single short clip. Compressed multi-action prompts are what cause rushed, unnatural motion.

wrong: fresh prompt for shot 2, no reference to shot 1
right: reuse the exact character, wardrobe, and environment description from shot 1, verbatim — change only the action line
never: Never reword a character or setting description between shots in one sequence. Every reworded detail is a new chance for identity drift.

right: no legible text anywhere in frame; if signage appears, keep it out of focus and under 10% of frame width
never: Never ask a video model to render legible on-screen text. Text rendering is not reliable in current video generation and will come out garbled — every time.

right: he runs across the field at a constant, even stride — steady frame-to-frame velocity, no sudden speed changes, no pose-to-pose teleporting
never: Never prompt movement without specifying a constant pace or easing. Speed left to the model’s discretion is what causes stutter, judder, and frame-skipping between poses.

wrong: she sets the phone on the table
right: she sets the same black phone — screen still lit, same orientation — down on the table's left edge; it stays exactly there, unmoved and unchanged, for the rest of the shot
never: Never let an object's position, count, or state go unanchored after it's introduced. Unanchored objects are what teleport between hands, duplicate, change appearance, or vanish between frames.
